analysis.one_liner: Gives student loan borrowers new servicing protections, fee limits, and disclosure rights.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on December 5, 2023, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a "bill of rights" for people repaying student loans, both federal and private. It would cap late fees, require clearer billing statements, force servicers to apply payments in the way that costs the borrower least, staff toll-free repayment specialists and military-veteran liaisons, ban forced arbitration, cancel private loans when a borrower dies or becomes disabled, and wipe bad default marks from credit reports once a loan is fixed. It would also put federal loan servicers under the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's rules.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million Americans repaying student loans, especially borrowers struggling with payments: they would get clearer statements, capped late fees (no more than 4% of the past-due amount, and never before 15 days), payments applied to the highest-interest loan by default, live help from trained repayment specialists before default, discharge of private loans on death or total disability, removal of default records from credit reports after rehabilitation or consolidation, and the right to sue in court instead of being forced into arbitration. Servicemembers and veterans would get dedicated liaisons and protection from credit damage while serving in combat zones.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers, including servicemembers and veterans

how_it_helps.text: Caps late fees at no more than 4% of the past-due payment, bars fees before a 15-day grace period, and bans charging multiple late fees for one late payment or per-loan fees for borrowers with several loans.

Requires servicers to apply payments on the date received and, unless the borrower says otherwise, direct extra payments to the loan with the highest interest rate first, saving borrowers money over the life of the loan.

Requires every servicer to staff a repayment specialist office with a toll-free number that must proactively contact borrowers who fall behind, offer alternatives to default (income-driven repayment, discharge, forgiveness programs) before placing a loan in default, and forbids paying that staff based on call volume or collections.

Bans mandatory predispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in student loan servicing, so borrowers could take servicers to court, and makes servicers legally liable for violations just like other creditors under consumer law.

Requires private student loans to be cancelled if the borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled, and creates a 9-payment rehabilitation path that wipes the charge-off and delinquency from a borrower's credit history.
Requires that once a defaulted federal loan is paid off or consolidated, the loan holder ask credit bureaus to remove the default from the borrower's credit history.

Gives each servicer a specially trained Servicemember and Veterans Liaison, bars charging off or reporting a loan while the borrower is on active duty in a combat zone, and bans denying credit to someone because they qualify for Servicemembers Civil Relief Act protections.

Brings federal loan servicers under the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and federal consumer financial law, requires them to answer complaints filed with any federal or state agency, and bars them from using borrower data to market other financial products.

Requires detailed monthly billing statements, plain-language disclosures before the first full payment is due, written notice 45 days before any loan is transferred or the interest rate rises, and a full loan history — including payments qualifying toward loan forgiveness — available to borrowers free of charge.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan servicers and private lenders bear the cost. Federal loan servicers (companies hired by the Education Department) would have to staff specialist units, extend service hours, build new disclosure and error-resolution systems, and forgo late-fee and collections revenue; private lenders would lose the ability to raise rates on existing balances, enforce arbitration clauses, and collect on loans after a borrower's death or disability. Some compliance costs could be passed back to borrowers through higher private loan rates or tighter lending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan servicers and private lenders

drawbacks.text: The rules are extensive and compliance-heavy: servicers must build new billing, disclosure, outreach, staffing, and error-resolution systems, and private lenders face new underwriting costs from mandatory death and disability discharge — costs that lenders say would show up as higher interest rates or fewer private loan options for students.

The bill does nothing to reduce what borrowers actually owe: it does not cap federal interest rates, forgive balances, or lower monthly payments — it makes servicing fairer but leaves the underlying debt untouched.

The bill itself delays its effective date by up to one additional year for federal loan servicers while the Education Department and the CFPB write implementing regulations, so the strongest protections would not arrive quickly even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the gains are concrete and large: capped fees, payments applied to their benefit rather than the servicer's, real help before default, court access instead of forced arbitration, and credit records cleaned up after a default is fixed. The costs fall on an industry whose business model has long included fee revenue and steering struggling borrowers into costly forbearance; some of those compliance costs may reach borrowers through private loan pricing, and the bill does nothing about the size of the debt itself. On balance the protections would have outweighed the costs for most borrowers, but the bill never got far enough for anyone to test that trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate education committee, which never gave it a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Student Loan Borrower Bill of Rights on December 5, 2023, with six Senate colleagues joining at introduction.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Eight senators — all Democrats — cosponsored the bill.
The HELP Committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers and private lenders are better off, since none of the fee limits, arbitration bans, or discharge requirements took effect. Borrowers struggling with payments gained nothing from the bill's death.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no action on it for the remaining thirteen months of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Majority Leader and Senate floor schedulers
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with the committee inactive, no vote ever occurred.

against.name: Student loan servicers and private lenders
against.role: Industry affected by the bill's fee limits, arbitration ban, and servicing mandates
against.what_they_did: No recorded position in the congressional record; the bill's requirements would have cut into servicer fee and collections revenue and lender interest income, and industry opposition to similar borrower-rights bills is well documented outside the record.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters — the sponsor and eight cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored, though the bill never reached a vote so no partisan roll-call exists.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers (contractors such as Nelnet/Aidvantage and MOHELA)
industries.note: Servicers are paid by the Education Department to manage federal loans; the bill would force them to staff specialist and military-liaison units, cap the late fees and collections activity they profit from, apply payments to the borrower's benefit, open themselves to lawsuits without arbitration shields, and answer to the CFPB. Its interest in this bill ran directly against borrowers'.

industries.industry: Private student lenders (such as Sallie Mae and SoFi)
industries.note: Private lenders would lose the ability to raise rates on existing balances, keep mandatory arbitration clauses, collect after a borrower's death or total disability, or charge fees for electronic payments — and would have to tell refinancing customers which federal protections they are giving up.

The bill requires servicers to try live outreach and repayment alternatives before default and bars collection activity while a borrower dispute is pending, shrinking the flow of defaulted loans assigned to collectors.

industries.industry: Credit reporting and consumer data industry
industries.note: The bill requires removal of default records after a loan is rehabilitated, consolidated, or paid off, and bars negative reporting during disputes and combat-zone service — reducing the data bureaus hold and report, though it does not otherwise change their business.
